papers.summary: LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed or stepped through. We argue that grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension with explorable theorems, a system that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging each step. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on that example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study ($n = 16$) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-reading task, participants who had access to the provided explorability features gave better, more correct, and more detailed answers to comprehension questions, demonstrating a stronger overall understanding of the underlying mathematics.

papers.title: Real-Time GPU-Accelerated Monte Carlo Evaluation of Safety-Critical AEB Systems Under Uncertainty
papers.summary: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) systems represent a safety-critical national interest, with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS No. 127) requiring AEB in all new light vehicles sold in the United States by September 2029. However, production implementations frequently rely on deterministic stopping-distance or Time-to-Collision (TTC) thresholds that fail to capture uncertainty in sensing, road conditions, and vehicle dynamics. This paper presents a GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo framework for stochastic evaluation of emergency braking performance using a longitudinal vehicle model incorporating aerodynamic drag, road grade, brake actuator dynamics, and weight transfer effects. A one-thread-per-sample execution strategy exploits the independence of Monte Carlo rollouts, while deterministic CPU-generated sampling ensures bit-exact numerical consistency between CPU and GPU implementations. The framework is evaluated across four hardware platforms: two laptop GPUs (GTX 1650, RTX 5070) and two automotive-grade embedded platforms (Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson AGX Orin). Peak speedups of 54.57x are achieved. Real-time feasibility analysis with a complete AEB timing budget demonstrates that the Jetson AGX Orin can execute approximately 25,000 Monte Carlo samples within a 530 ms budget, enabling real-time probabilistic AEB evaluation as part of a complete embedded pipeline. Collision probability analysis demonstrates that a threshold set at the mean stopping distance of 79.2 m leaves a collision probability of approximately 47%, while the conservative 1% risk threshold requires a minimum safe headway of 111.1 m, an additional 31.9 m (40%). These results provide quantitative guidance for risk-aware AEB threshold selection under the NHTSA final rule.

papers.title: Sequential vs. Synchronized Entanglement Swapping: QKD Secret-Key Rate under Optimized Link-Layer Control
papers.summary: Quantum repeater chains build long-distance entanglement for quantum key distribution (QKD) by creating pairs on short links and joining them through entanglement swapping. Because stored pairs lose fidelity while they wait, swap timing can affect the secret-key rate. We study how network-layer swap scheduling affects six-state QKD on a simulated four-hop chain under an idealized Werner-state noise model. We compare a sequential (swap-and-wait) discipline, which builds and stores partial chains, with a synchronized (wait-and-swap) discipline, which waits until all links are ready before swapping. Both use the same reinforcement-learned link controllers, isolating the effect of the swapping discipline. When stored pairs cannot retain sufficient fidelity for one network time step, our sequential implementation produces no key, while synchronized retains a small key rate from simultaneous link deliveries. Once sequential becomes viable, it outperforms synchronized by up to 19.1% in the homogeneous chains studied, with the advantage decreasing as memory lifetime increases. We predict the synchronized short-memory pair-delivery rate from link-delivery statistics and derive a closed-form condition for when sequential can preserve progress across time steps. We also examine chains with one slower link, where partial chains can wait and decay at the bottleneck. In this setting, synchronized slightly outperforms sequential at longer memory lifetimes. Moving the slow link has little effect on key rate away from the transition region but strongly affects sequential link-buffer occupancy. Choosing a swapping discipline therefore depends not only on whether memories can preserve partial progress, but also on how the link configuration determines where that progress must wait and decay.

papers.title: UPSim: UxNB Propagation Simulator for 3D Map-Driven FR3 Deployments
papers.summary: We introduce UPSim (UxNB Propagation Simulator), an open-source, Ray Tracing-calibrated solution for spatially consistent FR3 (16.95 GHz) air-to-ground propagation modeling in Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. Instead of executing point-to-point ray launches for every ground position, UPSim derives deterministic visibility regions directly from global 3D building geometry (3D-GloBFP) via fast shadow projection. It then augments these regions with Line-of-Sight (LOS) state-specific, UAV height- and distance-dependent path loss, spatially correlated large-scale fading, and log-logistic small-scale fading parameterized by over 136 million Ray Tracing (RT) channels. Validation against reference RT data demonstrates that UPSim accurately reproduces empirical attenuation maps, outperforming the 3GPP baseline by reducing the aggregate Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance from 0.33 to 0.04. The resulting maps enable route-based analysis of channel evolution in complex urban layouts, capturing critical trajectory-level metrics such as spatial outage persistence. Consequently, UPSim provides a highly scalable, open-source middle ground between computationally expensive full RT and purely stochastic models for mobility-aware 6G aerial network planning.

papers.title: Cover Semantics for Intuitionistic Modalities
papers.summary: Intuitionistic modal logic (IML) has inspired several developments in programming languages including modal type systems for staging, computational effects and language-based security. IMLs are typically studied using Kripke-style relational semantics, which simplifies proofs of meta-theoretic properties, such as completeness and consistency, by making it easy to construct models. Kripke-style relational semantics, however, relies upon classical reasoning principles, which makes it unappealing from a computational perspective and unsuitable for formalization in a constructive type theory. Goldblatt provides an alternative semantics for IMLs by extending Beth-Kripke-Joyal-style "cover" semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic with relations to support modalities. Goldblatt's "relational cover" semantics overcomes classical reasoning but introduces a new limitation: it relies upon a "modal localization" condition that restricts the class of models and complicates model construction. Goldblatt bypasses this restriction by using intricate order-theoretic completion arguments to prove completeness. In this article, we present a conservative extension of relational cover semantics that alleviates this restriction and is amenable to simpler and standard model construction techniques. We formalize our semantics in Agda and prove completeness constructively in the style of Normalization by Evaluation for a variety of IMLs featuring independent box and diamond modalities.

papers.title: Formalizing Flag Algebras in Lean
papers.summary: Razborov's flag algebra method is one of the most successful tools for proving asymptotic density inequalities in extremal graph theory. It reduces an inequality about all large graphs avoiding a forbidden pattern to finitely many algebraic conditions, and a certificate satisfying them can be found by semidefinite programming. We formalize the method for finite simple graphs in Lean 4, building on Mathlib. The formalization covers flags and their densities, the flag algebra as a quotient vector space, positive homomorphisms as limits of graph sequences, Razborov's random extensions, and the downward operator that averages out labels. On top of this theory, we build verified computation of flag densities and a tactic that turns certificates found by semidefinite programming into Lean proofs. The certificate serves only as candidate data; Lean checks every fact the proof uses. With this development we verify seven Tur\'an-type upper bounds. Adding lower-bound constructions proved in Lean yields the asymptotic form of Mantel's theorem and the asymptotic Erd\H{o}s pentagon theorem $\pi(C_5;K_3)=24/625$; to our knowledge, the latter has not previously been formalized in a proof assistant. We also prove two inequalities of Goodman. All density theorems reported here depend only on the standard axioms of Lean's logic. Formalization also led us to treat forbidden subgraphs with a different semantics. Instead of building a separate flag algebra for each forbidden family, we keep a single algebra of all graphs and impose the constraint only when interpreting an inequality, through randomly labeled limits of graphs satisfying it. We prove that this ensemble semantics yields the intended density bounds, and that a condition we call root-plantability characterizes when it agrees with the standard semantics.

papers.title: sGLP: Simulating People with Stochastic Agents
papers.summary: Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that are run by the participants. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed. Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour. We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate. We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.
